beats.narration_text: Hey, this is Param Madan, and this explainer video is on the verify step: how the physics engine checks its own answers. A solver can do perfect algebra on the wrong equation. So after SymPy answers, the engine asks one more question. Does this answer also come out right some other way?

props.command: After SymPy solves a problem, how does the physics engine check that the answer is actually right?
output: Plug the answer back into the equations
Reach it again by a different route

beats.narration_text: In the next few minutes, you'll see three things. First, the check every answer gets. Second, the stronger checks some cards carry, including laws of physics used as tests. And third, what the engine calls an answer when a check fails, or can't run. No physics or coding background needed.

The answer up front. Every answer is plugged back into its equations. Where it matters, it's also checked for being physically possible. And eleven of the thirty-one cards add a third check: an independent path to the same answer. If anything fails, the answer isn't hidden. It's labeled, flagged for review.

Check one: plug it back in. The engine substitutes the answer into the card's own equations, and measures what's left over. That leftover is called the residual. If it's essentially zero, the answer really satisfies the equations. It's simple, and it runs on every card, every time.

Check two: is it physically possible? Some quantities can't be negative: a speed, a time, a distance travelled. Cards mark those as must be positive. An answer that satisfies the algebra, but comes out negative, fails here. The algebra can be right while the physics is impossible.

beats.new_visual_element: the same answer by a different route
beats.narration_text: Check three is the strong one: reach the same answer by a different route. In a circuit, the two branch currents, one point two amps and one amp, must add up to the total, two point two. That's Kirchhoff's current law. A capacitor, after one time constant, must be about sixty-three percent charged. So a nine volt battery gives five point six nine volts. And an orbit's period is worked out again, from a second formula.

Some checks are laws of physics, used as tests. Escape speed must be exactly the square root of two times the orbital speed. A heat engine's efficiency must lie strictly between zero and one. A check like that doesn't just compare two numbers. It asks whether the answer obeys a rule that nature enforces.

Every result gets a label. Pass every check, and the status is verified. Fail any, and it's solved, but flagged for review: still shown, never passed off as checked. When the answer is in symbols, the numeric checks can't run, so the engine reports them as not run, instead of quietly passing them. And the limit: twenty of the thirty-one cards have no independent path yet.

So here's the takeaway. One answer is a claim. The same answer, reached two different ways, is evidence. When an A.I. model gives you a number, ask it to check the answer another way. If the two don't match, you've found the step to look at.
Your turn. Paste this into Claude with any problem it has already solved. It asks Claude to verify the answer three ways.

props.command: Here is a problem and an answer: [paste both]. Verify the answer three ways. 1: substitute it back into the original equations and show what is left over. 2: check it is physically possible: signs, sizes, units. 3: reach it by a different method. Say which checks pass and which fail.
output: Plugged back in: what's left over
